title: A deployment succeeds but old clients start receiving 500 responses
description: Diagnose and fix a breaking API change that causes old clients to receive 500 errors after a successful deployment, using versioning, feature flags, and contract testing.

data.text: You deploy a new version of an API. The deployment succeeds and health checks pass, but support tickets start flooding in from legacy mobile clients that receive 500 errors on every request. The new clients work fine. You need to determine why the old clients broke and how to prevent this from recurring without blocking feature delivery.

items: A required field was removed or renamed in the response body, and old clients fail to deserialize it
The API now returns a different HTTP status code for validation errors, and old clients treat it as a server error
Enum values were changed or removed, causing serialization exceptions on the server
A new dependency was added that is incompatible with the runtime version used by old clients
The server started returning JSON properties with different casing conventions
A middleware change introduced stricter authentication requirements that old clients do not satisfy

terms.definition: The property that newer versions of software continue to work with older clients or consumers.
A versioning scheme where breaking changes increment the major version number.
Tests where the consumer defines the expected API contract, and the provider verifies it.
Conditional logic that enables or disables functionality at runtime without redeploying.
Designing systems to provide limited functionality when some components fail.

data.text: The fastest way to confirm the cause is to compare the response schema between versions. Use a tool like tcpdump, Wireshark, or your API gateway logs to capture the raw response that old clients receive. Look for missing fields, type mismatches, or new required properties that were not present in the previous version.

data.title: Breaking response change
data.content: Version 1 returned a flat user object. Version 2 nests it under data.user:

items: Roll back the deployment if user impact is high and the fix is not immediately available.
Enable a feature flag that returns the old response shape to legacy user agents.
Add API versioning: route /v1/ to the old behavior and /v2/ to the new behavior.
Update the client version detection logic to serve the correct schema.
Add consumer-driven contract tests to your CI pipeline so this regression is caught before deployment.

cards.title: Rollback
cards.description: Revert the deployment to the previous working version.
cons: Does not fix the underlying contract mismatch

cards.title: Feature flag
cards.description: Toggle behavior at runtime based on client version or user segment.
cons: Flag debt if not cleaned up

cards.title: API versioning
cards.description: Expose multiple API versions simultaneously and route requests accordingly.

cards.title: Contract testing
cards.description: Automated tests that verify the provider meets consumer expectations.

data.caption: Diagnosis flow for breaking API changes after deployment
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Old clients get 500s] --> B[Capture raw response]
    B --> C{Response shape changed?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Compare schemas v1 vs v2]
    C -->|No| E{Status code changed?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Check error handling logic]
    E -->|No| G{Server exception logs?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Check enum or type changes]
    G -->|No| I[Check middleware or auth]
    D --> J[Add versioning or feature flag]
    F --> J
    H --> J
    I --> J
    J --> K[Add contract test to CI]

data.title: Do not rely on health checks alone
data.text: Health checks typically hit the newest client path or a synthetic endpoint that does not exercise legacy contracts. Always test with real client versions in a staging environment that mirrors production traffic before deploying breaking changes.

items: Additive-only changes during minor releases: new fields are optional, removed fields go through a deprecation cycle
Use OpenAPI or GraphQL schema validation to enforce compatibility in CI
Run integration tests with actual legacy client builds against every release candidate
Deprecate fields with a sunset header before removing them
Automate schema diffing as part of the pull request pipeline

items.question: How long should a deprecation period last?
items.answer: It depends on your client update cycle. Mobile apps may take weeks to propagate through app stores, so a 90-day deprecation window is common. For server-to-server APIs, 30 days is usually sufficient.

items.question: Should I version with URL paths or headers?
items.answer: URL path versioning (/v1/, /v2/) is the most explicit and easiest to route. Header-based versioning is cleaner but harder to debug from logs.

items.question: What if I cannot add contract tests immediately?
items.answer: Start with a single canary deployment that routes a percentage of legacy traffic to the new version and alerts on error rate. That buys you time to build proper contract tests.

data.title: Audit a service for breaking changes
data.description: Pick a service in your codebase. Review its last three releases and identify any changes that could break older clients. Document the risk and propose a mitigation for each.
steps: List the consumers of the service and their versions
Review pull requests merged since the last release for schema changes
Classify each change as additive, non-breaking, or breaking
For breaking changes, propose a deprecation or versioning strategy
Add one contract test that would have caught the most dangerous breaking change
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a compatibility audit that identifies hidden breaking changes and adds at least one automated safeguard.

data.title: Summary
points: Compare response schemas between versions to identify the breaking change
Use feature flags or API versioning to restore service quickly
Add consumer-driven contract tests to prevent recurrence
Treat deprecation as a first-class concern, not an afterthought
data.takeaway: A deployment is not successful if it breaks your oldest clients. Measure success by user impact, not just health-check status.
